Systems Programming and Machine Organization
Chapter 2: C and C++ for Systems Programming: values, bounds, and lifetime
Dr. Charles Dorner

1. A name, a value, and an owner are different things
Problem and first experiment

SAY
A pointer variable has a name and stores a pointer value. That alone does not tell us who owns the object it reaches, how many elements are available, or how long access remains valid. Those missing facts cause many systems defects. A function can copy a pointer parameter while still changing the original pointed-to integer. A function can also return a copied integer whose value survives after its local variables disappear. The chapter develops the language needed to distinguish these cases. Before reading syntax as a memory diagram, identify the actual objects, their types, the permitted range, and the component responsible for keeping them alive.

DO
Draw two pointer variables and one target object, then label the owner separately.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch2.json → SP02.003 / Core Distinctions

------------------------------------------------------------

2. Choose a result type that can represent every state
Problem and first experiment

SAY
A byte-reading interface may report a positive count, zero for end of input, or a negative error indication. Reducing those three cases to a boolean loses meaning before the caller can make a good decision. A zero-byte result is not automatically the same as failure. The chapter contrasts size_t, an unsigned size type, with signed result types used by some system interfaces. Choose the type and the checking order to preserve every required state. Only after recognizing an error should a caller convert a successful count into a size for indexing or allocation. This is interface design, not merely a preference for one integer spelling.

DO
List positive count, end of input, and failure as three separate states.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch2.json → SP02.010 / 2.1.4 Boolean Types

------------------------------------------------------------

3. A zero byte ends a string, not every payload
Problem and first experiment

SAY
The array contains A, a zero byte, B, and a final zero byte. strlen is safe here because a terminator exists, but it applies the string contract and returns one. The span deliberately describes the first three array elements as a binary payload, so its length is three and its third byte prints B. A span is a borrowed range: it stores access and a count, not ownership of the array. The array stays alive throughout main, which supports this use. Neither result is numerically wrong. The mistake would be choosing the string length when a binary protocol says all three payload bytes belong to the message.

DO
Predict both lengths and identify which contract each operation follows.

SOURCE
Lecture demonstration for content/systems-programming/ch2.json → SP02.008 / Text vs. Binary Buffers

------------------------------------------------------------

4. Validate a signed status before converting it
Problem and first experiment

SAY
This is a model of a fallible interface result, not a real read system call. result is negative one. Converting it to size_t is a defined unsigned conversion, but it produces the largest value of that unsigned type, which is certainly greater than one hundred. The first line therefore says converted looks large=true. The corrected branch checks negativity in the signed type and prints validated=error. It never treats that error as a count. A cast tells the compiler to perform a conversion; it does not certify that the resulting value is meaningful for the application. Maintainable boundary code keeps validation close to the conversion it justifies.

DO
Predict the boolean without depending on the platform’s exact size_t width.

SOURCE
Lecture demonstration for content/systems-programming/ch2.json → SP02.006 / ssize_t vs. size_t

5. Problem and first implementation
The chapter problem

SAY
Change one local copy and one borrowed object. Predict which updates the caller can see.

Begin with the complete chapter demonstration. It fixes the input so you can follow each change in state. After that trace is clear, the lab expands the contract: Write one function that returns a changed copy and one that changes the caller’s vector. Reject an empty vector before accessing its first element.

6. Where the simple approach fails
The chapter problem

SAY
A reference does not extend the vector’s lifetime. Returning a reference to a local vector would leave a dangling reference.

A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Remove & from change_in_place. The function changes only its local copy, and the caller still sees 2.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Use a reference for the in-place operation and a value parameter for the copy operation. Name the operations so a caller can see the difference.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch2.json → SYS02.02

7. Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
The chapter problem

SAY
A value parameter creates a separate vector object. A reference parameter, marked &, names the existing vector. The empty check is a precondition check performed before indexing; throwing leaves the original vector unchanged. Return-by-value lets the returned vector own its storage without a dangling reference.

A plausible alternative: Copy when independent data is required; borrow when the caller retains ownership and the lifetime is clear.

13. ssize_t vs. size_t
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A POSIX-style read can return a byte count or a negative error. ssize_t can represent both. Converting -1 to size_t too early creates a very large unsigned value. Validate first; convert successful counts second.

Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY

22. 2.2.1 Arrays
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
If base address is A and element size is s, element i begins at A + i and s. Built-in subscripting does not automatically enforce bounds. An array often converts to a pointer, but it is not itself a pointer object. std::array and std::vector preserve stronger sequence abstractions.

SAY

55. Chapter 2 Takeaways
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Types define value domains and participate in expression semantics. Pointers and references provide access—not automatic ownership or validity. Scope, storage duration, and object lifetime are distinct. Robust systems interfaces make bounds, ownership, status, and lifetime explicit. Next: bits, bytes, and binary data.

56. Preserve extent when an array crosses an interface
Reason about the implementation

SAY
An array of four integers contains four objects, but a function parameter written as an array commonly adjusts to a pointer parameter. Inside that function, sizeof measures the pointer rather than recovering the caller's array extent. Passing a separate count can be correct, but the pointer and count must describe the same live range. A span packages those facts together while still borrowing the storage. It does not automatically prevent every invalid operation: a span can outlive its owner if the program lets it escape. The safer interface preserves information needed for checking, while the lifetime contract still states how long that information is valid.

DO
Compare an array parameter, pointer-plus-count, and span for retained information.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch2.json → SP02.012 / Array Extent Can Disappear

------------------------------------------------------------

57. Value, reference, and pointer parameters change different objects
Reason about the implementation

SAY
Suppose a function receives int count by value and assigns nine to count. It changed its own parameter, not the caller's integer. With int& count, the assignment changes the caller's object through a reference. With int* count passed by value, assigning a new pointer changes only the local pointer, while assigning through *count changes the designated integer if access is valid. These are three distinct operations, not three spellings for the same effect. const can restrict mutation through a particular access path, but it does not describe cleanup ownership. Document whether a parameter is borrowed for the call, retained afterward, or consumed into a new owner.

DO
Trace reassignment of a pointer separately from assignment through its dereference.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch2.json → SP02.024 / C++ References as Parameters

------------------------------------------------------------

58. A tag and its active value must agree
Reason about the implementation

SAY
A message may hold either a count or text. A union can reuse storage for those alternatives, but storage overlap does not mean both values are independently alive. A separate tag must agree with the active member whenever code interprets the message. If the tag says text while only an integer has been established, casting or reading does not repair the missing lifetime relationship. In C++, std::variant combines a discriminator with managed alternative lifetimes when that abstraction fits. Raw unions still have uses at carefully controlled boundaries, but they require a more detailed invariant. Choose the simpler representation that makes invalid combinations hard to express.

DO
Describe a count-or-text message and ask which impossible state must be prevented.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch2.json → SP02.018 / 2.2.3 Unions

------------------------------------------------------------

59. Scope hides names; lifetime governs valid use
Reason about the implementation

SAY
Scope answers where a name can be used in source. Lifetime answers when the named object exists. A local owning handle can transfer its dynamic object to another owner before the local name disappears. A static local can preserve state between calls even though its name is visible only in that function. Conversely, returning a reference to an automatic local leaves a caller with access to an object whose lifetime ended. The pointer bits need not visibly change when that happens. This is why a non-null check is not a lifetime proof. Draw the object's start and end, then place every borrow inside that interval.

DO
Draw separate intervals for a function call, local handle, and transferred dynamic object.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch2.json → SP02.041 / 2.5.4 Scope vs. Lifetime

63. A value copy and a borrowed reference
Code, diagrams, and debugging

SAY
A value copy and a borrowed reference. auto asks the compiler to infer the type. No & appears, so copy is a separate vector with separate element storage.

Change one local copy and one borrowed object. Predict which updates the caller can see.

auto without & creates a separate vector here. The & in this declaration means reference: no second vector is created. Only the assignment through borrowed reaches the original. In the for loop, : means take each element from the range on the right.

auto asks the compiler to infer the type. No & appears, so copy is a separate vector with separate element storage.

auto& creates a reference: borrowed is another name for readings, not a second vector.

The [0] subscript selects the first element. Changing copy does not change readings.

The [1] subscript selects the second element. Writing through borrowed changes readings because both names reach the same vector.

The colon in this range-based for means take each element from readings in order. const int value makes a read-only value copy for that iteration; it is not a reference because there is no &. The stream prints each value followed by a space.

The copy has independent element storage; borrowed names readings itself. Both selected subscripts refer to live elements.

A reference does not extend the vector’s lifetime. Returning a reference to a local vector would leave a dangling reference. In the extended lab: Remove & from change_in_place. The function changes only its local copy, and the caller still sees 2.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.

74. Chapter summary and maintenance
Recall and transfer

SAY
A value parameter creates a separate vector object. A reference parameter, marked &, names the existing vector. The empty check is a precondition check performed before indexing; throwing leaves the original vector unchanged. Return-by-value lets the returned vector own its storage without a dangling reference.

Choose a simpler approach when its narrower contract is enough. Copy when independent data is required; borrow when the caller retains ownership and the lifetime is clear.

When this system changes, retain a check that exposes the known failure: Remove & from change_in_place. The function changes only its local copy, and the caller still sees 2. Use a reference for the in-place operation and a value parameter for the copy operation. Name the operations so a caller can see the difference.

content/systems-programming/ch2.json → SYS02.14

------------------------------------------------------------

75. Language layout is not an external format
Recall and transfer

SAY
A structure groups useful fields, but its raw bytes may also contain padding and pointer representations. A different compiler, ABI, or field order can change that layout. Writing sizeof(structure) bytes to a file therefore does not automatically create a stable format. Define the external fields, sizes, order, and accepted values explicitly, then encode them. On input, check the byte count and decode values before constructing a useful object. This separation also avoids accidentally publishing unnamed padding bytes. It costs a little boundary code, but it makes version changes and compatibility tests much clearer than depending on an accidental in-memory arrangement.

DO
Ask learners to list three properties an external format must state explicitly.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch2.json → SP02.017 / Structures Are Not Wire Formats

------------------------------------------------------------

76. Review an interface by the information it preserves
Recall and transfer

SAY
Take a function that receives a pointer and returns a number. Before judging its body, ask what the pointer may designate, whether it can be null, how many elements exist, who keeps them alive, and whether the function retains access after returning. Then ask what each result means and whether the result type can express every state. These questions turn language vocabulary into an interface review. A correct cast cannot repair a false count, and a successful compilation cannot prove a borrowed object is still alive. Good systems code supplies the missing contracts through types, validation, and clear documentation rather than leaving every caller to guess.

DO
Use the declaration as a short review exercise and ask for the missing promises.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch2.json → SP02.048 / Chapter 2 Takeaways
